title: The UMAP Feature Browser
takeaway: A screenshot of the interactive map the authors publish alongside the article: every dictionary direction from two autoencoder runs — 4,608 of them — projected onto a plane, with a searchable list of human-written feature labels beside it. It establishes that the qualitative families of features the paper describes in prose are also tight geometric clumps, and that features from the small run and the large run land in the same clumps. It is a browsing tool, not a measurement: the clusters carry the meaning, the coordinates do not.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is a screenshot of a live page, not a static plot. Each dot in the right pane is one learned [[feature]] — more exactly one [[feature-direction]], a single column of the decoder matrix $W_d$ that the paper also calls the [[dictionary-decoder]].

Those columns live in the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. Each is held to unit length, so a column is a pure direction with no magnitude of its own.

Two [[dictionary-learning-run]]s are drawn together here. All 512 features of run A/0 and all 4,096 of run A/1 go into the same embedding, giving $512 + 4096 = 4608$ dots. Names follow the paper's [[feature-notation]]: `A/1/776` means transformer A, run 1, feature number 776.

### How to read it

The right pane is a two-dimensional [[umap]] embedding of those 4,608 vectors, fit with cosine distance. Both axes are UMAP coordinates. They carry no units, no scale and no meaning of their own.

What the embedding tries to preserve is neighbourhood. Two dots sit close when their dictionary vectors point in nearly the same direction. So read the clumps, not the positions — and do not read the gap between two clumps as a distance.

The left pane is the same set as a scrollable list. Each row shows a feature id and a short human-written label. Rows are grouped under a cluster number produced by [[hdbscan-feature-clustering]], and the list order comes from [[one-dimensional-umap-ordering]]; the cluster numbers themselves are just tags.

### What it shows

The three visible groups are thematic. Cluster #49 gathers citation features, #42 section references, #43 formatting and figure references. Several labels have the shape `"ref" in [context]`, which is the paper's notation for [[token-in-context-features]].

Two things follow. Each cluster mixes A/0 and A/1 ids, so a coarse feature from the small run sits beside the finer run-1 features covering the same ground — the geometric face of [[feature-splitting]]. And the families the paper argues for in prose show up as [[feature-geometry-clusters]], meaning conceptually similar features have small angles between their vectors.

One row reads `[Ultralow density cluster]`, a stand-in label for a member of the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] the authors treat as a training artifact rather than a real feature.

terms.definition: A dimensionality-reduction method that places high-dimensional points in a low-dimensional space while trying to keep each point near the same neighbours it had before. Here it takes 512-dimensional feature directions down to two coordinates for display.
Fitting one UMAP to the features of two different runs at once, rather than one map per run. It is what lets an A/0 dot and an A/1 dot be compared for closeness on the same picture.

The first field of a feature id: which of the two one-layer transformers the features were learned from. The paper trains transformers A and B with identical hyperparameters and different random seeds, and studies A throughout.
The second field, naming a dictionary learning run: the 512-feature autoencoder trained on transformer A's MLP activations. It is the smallest run in the A/0…A/5 sequence.
The 4,096-feature autoencoder trained on the same activations, eight times wider than A/0. It is the run the paper discusses most and recommends readers start with.
The full three-field identifier: transformer, run, then feature index inside that run. The paper writes transformer neurons differently, as A/neurons/32, so the two are never confused.
One learned direction in MLP activation space, produced by the sparse autoencoder and hoped to correspond to a single human-interpretable thing. Each dot on the map is one.

The unit vector in the 512-dimensional neuron space along which a feature writes when it fires — one column of the decoder matrix $W_d$. These columns, not the feature's activations, are what UMAP is run on here.
The autoencoder's output weight matrix. The paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" for the same object, and its columns are the feature directions plotted here.
The distance UMAP is given: it compares vectors by the angle between them and ignores their lengths. Since the dictionary columns are already unit-norm, this is the natural choice.
The column holding the group heading for each block of rows. Every listed feature belongs to exactly one such group, or to none.
Group identifiers assigned by HDBSCAN run on a separate 10-dimensional UMAP of the same features. The numbers are arbitrary labels, not a ranking or an ordering.
The column holding each row's feature id. The unlabelled column to its right holds that feature's written explanation.

A short human-written description of what the feature appears to respond to, such as "Years in some citation notation". These are interpretations attached by the authors for browsing, not measured quantities.
A text box that filters the left-hand list by the words in those written labels. It is how a reader finds, say, every feature whose description mentions "citation".
The label shape used for a feature that fires on one particular token but only inside a particular kind of surrounding text. [context] is a placeholder standing in for whatever that context is.

A placeholder label rather than an interpretation: it marks a feature that fires on roughly one token in ten million and that the authors say is almost never interpretable. They treat such features as an artifact of autoencoder training.
Labels that are just a literal string mean the feature mainly fires on that token. These sit in the same clusters as the longer prose labels, which is the point being made.
Fragments of Markdown section-anchor syntax appearing in cluster #42's labels. They show that the cluster is organised around a specific textual convention, not a broad topic.
Fragments of Markdown citation syntax appearing in cluster #49's labels. Features keyed to different pieces of the same citation format end up adjacent on the map.

A label naming what the feature does to the output as well as what it responds to: it fires in a citation and pushes up the probability of a year token. The paper notes every feature in a one-layer model can be read both as an input detector and as an action.
One feature's dictionary direction, placed at its two UMAP coordinates. All dots are drawn identically; nothing about a dot's size or colour encodes information here.
The two UMAP output coordinates. They are unnamed and unnumbered on purpose — the embedding has no preferred orientation, origin or scale, so the numbers would mean nothing.
Evenly spaced reference lines in the scatter pane. They help judge relative separations while panning and zooming; they do not mark meaningful values.

The subset of dots printed with their feature id, so a viewer can read identities without hovering. Labels are placed where there is room and can overlap, so some of the printed ids collide and are hard to read.
Toggles whether the mouse wheel zooms the scatter. Off by default so the wheel scrolls the page instead of the plot.
View controls for the scatter pane. "home" restores the full view of all 4,608 points after a reader has zoomed into a cluster.
A density-based clustering algorithm that finds groups of varying shape and leaves outlying points unassigned. It supplies the cluster numbers in the left pane.

The observation that as the dictionary grows, one broad feature is replaced by a family of narrower ones covering roughly the same ground. On this map it appears as A/0 and A/1 features sharing a cluster.

numbers.meaning: The number of features in run A/1, all of which are plotted. It is the dictionary size chosen for that run — eight times the width of the MLP being decomposed, which is what makes the dictionary overcomplete.

The number of features in run A/0, all of which are also plotted. This run is deliberately set to exactly the number of MLP neurons, so it is the smallest dictionary that is not compressing the layer.

The length of every dictionary column before UMAP, because the autoencoder reconstructs the 512 MLP neuron activations of the one-layer transformer. Same number as A/0's size, but a different quantity.
The total dot count in the scatter, from $512 + 4096$. Both runs go into one embedding so that features from different dictionary sizes can be compared for proximity.
The number of UMAP output dimensions, which is why the display is a plane. The paper also fits a 10-dimensional embedding, but only for clustering, and a 1-dimensional one for list order.

The UMAP hyperparameter setting how many nearest neighbours define each point's local structure. Larger values preserve more global shape at the cost of local detail; 15 is the value the paper reports for this embedding.
The UMAP hyperparameter controlling how tightly points may pack together in the output. A small value like this lets clusters compress into dense blobs, which is why the clumps here look solid.
Not a count but the distance setting: similarity is angle between dictionary vectors. This is the choice that makes "nearby on the map" mean "similar feature direction".
The HDBSCAN setting for the smallest group that counts as a cluster. Three is permissive, so even a small family of two split features plus their parent can be named a cluster.
The separate UMAP embedding that the clustering is actually run on, and its packing parameter. Clustering in 10 dimensions rather than 2 avoids letting the flattening to a plane decide the groups.

numbers.value: 0 and 1 (the middle field of an id)
numbers.meaning: The run index. A/0…A/5 form a sequence at fixed L1 coefficient with increasing dictionary size, so a larger index means a wider dictionary here.

The range of the third field of a feature id, one per hidden unit of the corresponding autoencoder. An index like 3898 is only a slot number and carries no ordering — feature 3898 is not in any sense larger or later than feature 357.

The three group headings visible in the left pane. They come from HDBSCAN's arbitrary labelling, so 42 and 43 being adjacent numbers is not why they are adjacent in the list — the list order comes from a one-dimensional UMAP.

numbers.value: about $10^{-7}$ (roughly one token in ten million)
numbers.meaning: The firing rate that defines the ultralow density cluster referenced by one row's label. The paper reports almost none of these features are interpretable, in contrast with the high density mode around $10^{-5}$.
